cur:catacombs2-aix-saint-mitre.summary: In a single crowded frieze before a backdrop of arcades, Christ stands at the centre with his right hand raised, while to his left Peter shoulders a long cross; two small figures kneel at their feet. The apostles approach from both sides in procession, each raising a hand in acclamation of their Lord. The lid carries a frieze of small winged figures around a central wreath.
facts: Tradition holds that the sarcophagus received the body of Saint Mitrius (Mitre), the martyr venerated in Aix; the Commons description dates it to the end of the 4th century.
It is the most notable piece in the lapidary collection kept in the chapel that forms the narthex of the cathedral's baptistery.
cur:catacombs2-aix-saint-mitre.notes: The scene is described from the photograph; the composition with Peter carrying the cross belongs to the family of 'Traditio Legis' sarcophagi.

cur:monumental2-saqqara-virgin-enthroned.summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a jewelled throne with the Christ Child on her lap, both looking straight out; two youthful archangels raise their hands in acclamation on either side, and two elderly saints stand at the ends, one holding a book. Fragmentary Greek or Coptic labels survive above the heads. The flat, brightly coloured figures are known here through the colour plate of the 1912 excavation report.
facts: The picture is a colour plate from Quibell's 1912 report on the Monastery of Apa Jeremias, whose monks' cells were decorated with prayer-niche paintings of Christ, the Virgin and the monastery's founders.

links.label: Internet Archive: Quibell, Excavations at Saqqara (1912)

cur:monumental2-saqqara-virgin-enthroned.notes: The image is a 1912 colour reproduction rather than a photograph. The inscription at the left appears to begin with the name of Apa Jeremias, but the saints' identities were not confirmed.

feat:kongo-crucifix-nkangi-kiditu.summary: A Christ rendered in a distinctly Kongo idiom hangs on a cross bordered with incised patterns, while small figures perch on the ends of the crossbar and sit above and below him. Kongo's ruler was baptized in 1491, and over the following centuries its artists recast the European crucifix in local forms and meanings. Such crucifixes are thought to have served both as objects of Christian devotion and as emblems of authority held by rulers and judges.
facts: The Kikongo name nkangi kiditu is usually explained as joining 'Kiditu' (from the Portuguese Cristo) with a word related to kanga, which can mean both 'to bind' and 'to save or protect.'

After King Afonso I's victory in 1509 Catholicism became the state religion of the ruling elite, and because ordained clergy were always scarce, Kongo's church relied heavily on Kongolese lay teachers (mestres) for centuries.
Some scholars have suggested that the cross resonated with an existing Kongo cosmogram representing the crossing between the world of the living and the world of the dead.
The small attendant figures, often shown in prayer, are a Kongo addition; they have been read as mourners, saints, or ancestors.
